title: Grid Filling
solution: Cells inside one piece are already distinct, so only pairs of cells that touch across a cut can clash. Let a be the row-strip heights and b the column-strip widths. If some row strip has height 1, that strip is a 1D sequence of pieces of widths b_j: a width-1 piece must be [1], and a width-2 piece is [1 2] or [2 1]. Two width-1 pieces with only width-2 pieces between them are impossible, because the orientation is forced all the way along and hits a 1 next to a 1. The same holds for columns. So the answer is -1 exactly when (some a_i=1 and b has two 1s separated only by 2s) or (some b_j=1 and a has two 1s separated only by 2s). A CSP brute force over every configuration up to 63 cells agrees with this. Sufficiency comes from a construction. First transpose if needed so that whenever b contains a 1, a contains one too. Then fill every a x b piece column-major in contiguous blocks: local column y receives the value range [(tau(y)-1)a+1, tau(y)a] for a permutation tau of 1..b. Horizontal neighbours lie in the same row strip, so their blocks are aligned. Picking tau_left(last) != tau_right(first) therefore gives the touching columns disjoint ranges, and that is a 1D problem. If both a and b contain 1s (both are then 1D-ok), use one tau per column strip: width 1 is [1]; width 2 is [1 2] left of the 1 in its run of 1s and 2s and [2 1] right of it; width >=3 is (3,...,b,1,2). If b has no 1s, thin rows alternate between tau = identity and tau = cyclic shift (2..b,1), and every other row uses identity. Vertical constraints then split per global column into a chain of row-strip segments, each owning a fixed block (size 1: one value, size 2: two orientations, size >=3: free top and bottom). A 3-state chain DP picks the top and bottom values. The DP always succeeds: a thin value can collide with a 2-block only when it equals 1, and then the chain is the 1D problem on a, which is 1D-ok; stacked thin rows and thin rows around a run of 2-strips get different values from the identity/shift alternation. Runtime is O(nm).

solution_check.how: Python solution (column-major block construction + per-column chain DP, with transpose) run on all 4 samples: every grid it printed passed a validity checker (each piece is a permutation of 1..x, adjacent cells differ), and it printed -1 on sample 4 as expected. Wrote a C++ CSP brute force (forward checking + MRV) for feasibility and compared it exhaustively on all 113,665 cut configurations with n,m<=9 and n*m<=63: feasibility matched in every case (37,076 feasible) and every printed grid validated. Ran 15,000 random configurations up to 14x14 (strips of size 1-7) against the brute force with 0 mismatches. Ran about 70 large random tests up to 1000x1000 with checker validation, plus a worst case of 1000x1000 with 500x500 strips (0.24 s).

notes.solver: constructive-algorithm: the problem asks for any valid filling, and the core of the solution is the column-major block construction plus the -1 characterization (from a forced-orientation argument in 1D). Considered and rejected: dynamic-programming / dp-on-dag (the per-column 3-state chain DP is a convenience, since explicit orientation rules give the same result, and nobody searching DP wants this problem); greedy (no exchange or greedy-choice argument, only forced propagation); parity-argument (a checkerboard-parity idea fails on odd-area pieces with corners of different colours and is not what decides feasibility); two-sat (the orientation of small pieces is boolean but never needs 2-SAT); bipartite-matching (Hall-style reasoning came up in analysis but the final construction is explicit). Tags: grid/matrix for the setting, permutation because every piece is a permutation of 1..x, implementation for the casework (transpose, three tau rules).
notes.skeptic: SOLUTION: correct. I derived the impossibility rule on my own and it agrees with the proposal. In a height-1 strip, each 1x2 piece between two 1x1 pieces is forced to [2 1] going away from the first 1, so it ends next to the second 1, whatever the run length. Nothing else in 2D ever makes a case infeasible: the brute force agrees on every config with n,m<=7. The construction works because touching columns of horizontal neighbours get disjoint value blocks whenever tau_left(last) != tau_right(first). Vertically, each global column is a chain of segments: size 1 is fixed, size 2 has two orientations, size 3 or more has free ends. A chain can only fail on thin, 2..2, thin with the same thin value in the block. When both a and b contain 1s, that happens only for block 1, which is exactly the heights 1,2*,1 case already ruled out. When b has no 1s, the identity/shift alternation gives consecutive thin rows different values. I confirmed all of this empirically (see skeptic_check). PATTERNS: constructive-algorithm KEEP. The output is a witness grid, and the whole difficulty is building it (column-major contiguous blocks with chosen tau) plus proving the -1 rule. GREEDY (judge tag) REJECTED, not added. No greedy-choice step carries the solution. The width-2 orientation rule ('orient away from the 1 in the run') is forced propagation that needs to see the whole run, not a local greedy choice. Naive greedies fail on many feasible inputs: cell-wise smallest-fit fails 1,596 of 6,280 feasible configs up to 7x7 (e.g. two height-1 rows over width 3: [1 2 3]/[2 1 3] clashes), and piece-wise first-fit over row/col-major, flip and reverse fills fails 3,108 (e.g. widths 1,3,1 need [2 1 3]). PARITY-ARGUMENT REJECTED. The -1 proof is forced orientation and does not depend on run-length parity: 1,1 and 1,2,1 and 1,2,2,1 all fail. The obvious checkerboard idea (odd values on one colour) is neither sufficient nor what decides feasibility. Odd x odd pieces with corners on different colours are unavoidable, and widths 1,3 with n=1 still work as [1][2 1 3]. DYNAMIC-PROGRAMMING / DP-ON-DAG REJECTED. The per-column chain 'DP' is a 2-6 state convenience that explicit orientation rules replace, as the proposal's both-1s case shows. Nobody searching DP wants this problem. Also not two-sat, bipartite-matching or hall-theorem: the final construction is explicit. TRAP binary-search-answer: does not apply. There is no optimisation and no monotone feasibility predicate; the answer is a fixed construction or -1, found in O(nm). TRAP bitmask-dp vs interval-dp: does not apply. There is no DP at all, and n,m up to 1000 with O(nm) output rules out any subset or interval state. The near-miss to watch here is constructive vs greedy, settled above. TAGS: grid and matrix (setting), permutation (each piece is a permutation of 1..x, and the construction picks per-strip permutations tau), implementation (transpose plus three tau rules plus the chain fill; the judge tags it too), constructive-algorithm. All kept. SUMMARY: 69 words, third person, accurate, gives the n,m<=1000 / sum constraint, and states the 1,2*,1 rule that drives the solution. Kept verbatim.
